answer.question: What should I bring to a Jacksonville turf estimate?
answer.answer: Bring the part of the yard you want to change, your intended use and any property plan or community requirements. Show us trees, narrow access, wet areas and drainage features. For a historic, pond-side or waterfront property, include any applicable review conditions before the layout is finalized.

blocks.h2: Keep the patio, garage route and trees working together.
paras: In a narrow yard, a pet area can follow the route from the door while leaving seating and planting intact. A green needs useful putting lines and space to stand, rather than extra cups in every corner. Show us the narrowest gate and existing paved edges.

For a property in the Riverside Avondale historic district, ask City preservation staff whether the site change needs a Certificate of Appropriateness. Obtain any required tree certification before planning turf beneath a mature canopy.

blocks.h2: Mark the canopy before placing the surface.
paras: Where Florida’s residential standard applies, turf inside a tree’s drip line needs a certified arborist’s finding that the installation will not harm the tree. Keep suitable planting or mulch there unless the required certification is obtained.
Discuss pet cleanup and leaf removal alongside the footprint. If a wet area or odor problem is already present, its cause and any additional work need to be considered separately from turf selection.

blocks.h2: Leave water routes and maintenance access clear.
paras: Bring the property plan and mark swales, pond edges and easements. The applicable state standard keeps turf out of swales, ditches and pond littoral areas and generally requires a 10-foot waterbody separation, with a seawall or bulkhead exception. Confirm those boundaries before choosing the usable turf area.

For a golf-facing, shared or association property, obtain the actual community requirements. A fenced yard should not automatically be assumed private from every relevant viewpoint, and an association’s response does not resolve all public requirements.

blocks.h2: Along the river, the oaks win. Turf doesn't have to fight them.
paras: Riverside was built out between 1901 and the late 1920s, mostly bungalows on narrow, deep lots around 50 feet wide. The fenced back yard behind one is often only 300 to 600 square feet, and it's usually in shade. The Cummer Oak on the riverfront is thought to be 400 to 450 years old, with a canopy 138 feet across (Cummer Museum), and trees like it hang over back fences all through the neighborhood. Grass can't grow under that, and many of these houses never had a sprinkler system to try. Turf doesn't need sun, and in shade it stays far cooler in summer.

The ground is the other half of the job. Jacksonville sits about 3 feet above sea level and gets roughly 52 inches of rain a year (Geography of Jacksonville), and the blocks near the river are flat, filled and slow to drain. We prepare the site and build the base for your soil, so rain goes down and away instead of sitting under the turf. Exterior work in the Riverside Avondale historic district needs a Certificate of Appropriateness from the City, so ask the Historic Preservation Commission whether your plan needs one before the layout is final (Riverside Avondale Preservation).

San Marco and San Jose, across the river, share the shade and the low edges. San Marco was laid out in 1925 (San Marco), its blocks grade down to the St. Johns, and the lowest yards hold water; its Treaty Oak, about 250 years old, shades a circle roughly 190 feet across. San Jose, planned the same year around a Donald Ross golf course, has real contour, which is ground a putting green can use for break. Its lower lots toward the river and Goodby's Creek stay wet, so either way the base does the work.

blocks.h2: Mandarin sand: scorched in April, soggy by September.
paras: There's a USDA soil series named Mandarin, first described in 1977 with its type location in Duval County. It's fine sand all the way down, somewhat poorly drained, with a seasonal high water table 18 to 42 inches below the surface for about half the year (USDA). The sand holds nothing in the dry months, then the water rises and the low corner goes soft. Add the moss-draped live oaks along Mandarin Road, with their shade, surface roots and leaf drop, and grass struggles to hold on at all.

Mandarin is flat, too, so there's no natural fall to borrow: drainage has to be built into the base. Beauclerc, just north, sits on the same sand, with Goodby's Creek on one side and Craven Creek running through, so its low lots are wet as well. The muddy patch by the back door, the worn stripe along the fence and the bare ground under the swing set all come from that wet sand. Pet turf drains when the dog goes and after a storm, and it's non-toxic, lead-free and safe for kids and pets.

Mandarin has no country club of its own, and many of its 1970s to 1990s back yards run 60 by 70 to 90 by 100 feet, room for a green with several cups. Southside, the office, shopping and medical district north of Mandarin, is a different job: flatwoods sand over a shallow water table, stormwater ponds threaded through everything built since 1990, fill pads that settle, and ground that compacts under heavy foot traffic. That's where commercial turf fits. Non-residential property there waters on Tuesdays and Fridays under the standard rule, and on Tuesdays only under the 2026 order.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Jacksonville, FL?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, pet turf and backyard putting greens across Jacksonville, FL. Three rules shape the job: the City can't ban turf on a single-family lot that meets Florida's standard; an HOA can't restrict turf that can't be seen from the street, a neighbor's lot, a common area or a community golf course; and a 2026 water shortage order has cut lawn watering to one day a week. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: Can the City of Jacksonville ban artificial turf?
faq.a: Not on a single-family lot of an acre or less, if the turf meets the state standard. Jacksonville is one consolidated city and county, so one code covers every neighborhood on this page, and state law has kept it from banning compliant turf since May 2026. That protection doesn't reach condominiums, parks, athletic fields or commercial property, and it doesn't override your HOA (DEP).

No. The state's Florida-Friendly Landscaping laws protect living landscapes, and UF/IFAS says that because synthetic turf isn't alive, it doesn't meet the program's criteria (UF/IFAS). Those laws won't help you with an HOA. Fla. Stat. 720.3045 is the one that does.

faq.q: When can I water a lawn in Jacksonville?
faq.a: JEA supplies the water and the St. Johns River Water Management District sets the days. Normally that's two days a week in daylight saving time and one in winter: odd or unnumbered addresses Wednesday and Saturday, even Thursday and Sunday, never between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. (SJRWMD). The Phase III shortage order in force when we checked on 7 September 2026 cuts that to Saturday for odd addresses and Sunday for even, nothing between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., and no more than an hour per zone (SJRWMD). The restrictions reach private wells and pumps too (Clay County Utility Authority). Turf needs none of it.

faq.q: What infill goes under turf in Jacksonville?
faq.a: On a single-family lot of an acre or less, natural infill only: clean silica sand, rock, shell or other natural material. Rubber and other synthetic infill are allowed only under playground equipment (Rule 62-308.100). In one lab study MRSA lasted longer in sand than in rubber, so a dog run wants a regular rinse. Our Florida infill guide has the detail.

faq.q: Does JEA give a rebate for artificial turf?
faq.a: Not that we could find: the water district's published material documents no artificial-turf rebate. Ask JEA directly before you count on one either way.
